answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: These lines open the final verse paragraph of “Little Gidding,” the fourth and final poem in Eliot’s Four Quartets — they are not the poem’s close, which runs on to “And the fire and the rose are one.” “Little Gidding” first appeared in the New English Weekly in October 1942 and was collected with the other three quartets in 1943. The wording matches the text as quoted in standard reference sources; we have not yet checked it against a first-edition scan.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: October 1942 (New English Weekly); Faber & Faber pamphlet, 1 December 1942; collected in Four Quartets (New York, 1943; London, 1944)

source.excerpt:
We shall not cease from exploration
And the end of all our exploring
Will be to arrive where we started
And know the place for the first time.
trail: Eliot finished “Little Gidding” by 19 September 1942, and it first appeared that October in the New English Weekly, per the Wikipedia entry on the poem ↗. Faber & Faber then issued it as a separate first-edition pamphlet (Gallup A42) on 1 December 1942, per first-edition bibliographic listings ↗.
All four quartets were then collected as Four Quartets, published in New York in 1943 and London in 1944, confirmed by the Wikipedia entry on Four Quartets ↗.

These lines are not the end of the poem. “Little Gidding” closes on “And the fire and the rose are one,” quoted as the poem’s final lines in Dallas Baptist University’s scholarly introduction to the poem ↗; the Wikipedia entry ↗ likewise describes further material after this passage.

The four-line wording as it circulates online can be seen on a Goodreads quote page crediting Little Gidding, Four Quartets ↗. That is a user-contributed aggregator — a record of popular usage, not a text authority. We have not yet collated the lines against a first-edition scan or an authorised Faber text.
source.excerptNote: These four lines open the final verse paragraph of “Little Gidding”; the poem continues past them to its last line. The popular quotation runs the first three lines together as one sentence and stops short of the fourth, “And know the place for the first time.” Quoted here in short extract for criticism and review.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: These lines open the final verse paragraph of “Little Gidding,” the fourth of Eliot’s Four Quartets, meditating on time, memory, and spiritual return — the idea that a journey outward ends in a renewed, deeper recognition of where one began. The poem does not stop here: it runs on to close on “And the fire and the rose are one.”

Eliot wrote the poem during the Second World War while serving as an air-raid warden in London; “Little Gidding” takes its title from the Anglican religious community in Huntingdonshire that Eliot visited in 1936.
context.pull: And the end of all our exploring will be to arrive where we started and know the place for the first time.
